scenario: AITA for calling the police on my daughter to teach her a lesson about stealing? | My daughter is in the sixth grade. Every morning, I have her take a couple of dollars out of my wallet for lunch money. In the last few weeks, several times I have noticed that I am missing a little bit more money than usual. So, this week, I planted a 20 dollar bill before my daughter took her lunch money out. Sure enough, she took it. I called the police and asked them to come with me to the school so that we could teach my daughter a lesson. Two officers met me there and we pulled my daughter out of class, after which she informed one of the officers that there has been a bully who is stealing her lunch money/forcing my daughter to buy her lunch. She also has been buying lunch for one of her friends who can not afford it. This was confirmed by both the bully, and the friend. My daughter was silent on the way home and i informed her that I was just trying to teach her a lesson, that stealing is wrong and can get you in a lot of trouble. and that in the future she needs to speak to myself or her mother if there are issues at school and we would be happy to help her resolve them. When we got home, my wife absolutely lost her shit on me, in full tears, telling me that this is a one way ticket to estrangement from our daughter in the future and that we should have just asked her why she was stealing money. She would have just lied about stealing in the first place so I really don’t understand what her idea of a solution is. My daughter apparently told my wife that she is terrified that her bully will now retaliate, and also that she may have lost her friend for bringing so much attention to her financial issue. She apologized for stealing and said she just didn’t want us to intervene. I am wondering if I really did the wrong thing here. AITA?

prediction.raw: 1 **Why:** - **Overreaction & Lack of Context:** Sixth grade (ages 11–12) is a critical developmental stage where children need guidance, not criminalization. The parent assumed theft was voluntary without investigating *why* the money was missing. The daughter was being **coercively forced by a bully** and helping a friend in need—**not stealing for personal gain**. Involving police for a child in this situation is disproportionate and trauma-inducing. - **Harm Over Lesson:** Pulling a child out of class in front peers, involving law enforcement, and framing it as "teaching a lesson" created fear, shame, and potential retaliation from the bully. It damaged trust with both parents and peers, as the daughter feared losing her friend and facing further harassment. - ** missed opportunity for support:** The correct approach would have been to **talk calmly with the daughter**, involve school counselors to address the bullying, and work with the family to resolve financial stress. Police involvement is reserved for *actual* criminal behavior (e.g., shoplifting, theft from a store), not a child’s response to coercion or poverty. - **Parental Responsibility:** A parent’s role is to *protect* and * guide*, not weaponize authority. The mother’s tears and the daughter’s terror confirm this was a catastrophic misstep. The "lesson" taught was that parents will call the cops over minor issues, not that "stealing is wrong"—which is a distinction the child already understood (she apologized). **Final verdict:** You are the asshole (YTA). This was a harmful overreaction that ignored the real problem (bullying) and prioritized punishment over empathy. Always investigate *why* before acting. **Correct next steps:** Apologize to your daughter, involve school authorities to address the bully, and work with a counselor to rebuild trust. Never involve police for a child’s non-criminal behavior without professional guidance.
